title: Hubble's near-infrared camera digs for galactic gold
caption: The Hubble Ultra Deep Field in near-infrared light, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Hubble Ultra Deep Field, HUDF · constellation Fornax
credit: NASA, ESA and R. Thompson (Univ. Arizona)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Galaxies scatter across this infrared view, and many of them are very far away and seen as they were long ago. It belongs to the Hubble Ultra Deep Field survey, described at the time as the deepest portrait of the Universe ever made. The view is a narrow core sample reaching across billions of light-years.

The picture comes from Hubble's Near Infrared Camera and Multi-Object Spectrometer. It looks a little farther back in time than the visible-light view of the same field. As space expands, light from remote galaxies is stretched from visible into infrared wavelengths, and some is absorbed by hydrogen between galaxies. The most distant galaxies therefore show up only in infrared.
By comparing infrared and visible images, astronomers hoped to find galaxies from perhaps 400 million years after the Big Bang, when the Universe had reached just 2 to 5 percent of its current age.

understand.summary: This composite combines Hubble's near-infrared NICMOS observations at 1.1 and 1.6 μm with visible-light data from the Advanced Camera for Surveys. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, and in ground-based photographs this patch of sky looks largely empty.

explore: From the ground, this patch of Fornax looks largely empty, and it spans just one-tenth the diameter of the full Moon. Only a handful of Milky Way stars appear in it. Looking into it is like peering through a 2.5 meter-long soda straw. Visible-light data from the Advanced Camera for Surveys were added to help tell the galaxies' colors apart.
alt: A field sprinkled with many small, distant galaxies.
